title: A school child has just figured out what AI can do to his classmate
author: The Slow AI
summary: This article documents the emergence of AI-generated child sexual abuse material in schools and argues that the technological infrastructure enabling it -- nudify apps, app store distribution, Section 230 liability protections -- constitutes what the author calls 'rape culture's next infrastructure.' The article opens with the documented pattern in UK secondary schools where the Internet Watch Foundation classified 150 AI-generated images from one school as criminal CSAM, made by pupils of pupils; UK schools have now been instructed by the National Crime Agency to remove student photographs from public websites. The 2023 Almendralejo, Spain case saw 20+ girls aged 11 and up targeted by classmates using the ClothOff app; the Spanish court's maximum sanction was 1,200 euros reduced for prompt payment -- while ClothOff continues to operate. The structural analysis centers on the 'Motherless precedent': 18 years of documented harm under Section 230 protection, ended not by regulators but by press investigation. The author catalogs the current app store reality: 47 nudify apps were found in Apple's App Store and 55 in Google Play in early 2026, with 483 million combined downloads and $122 million in revenue. The piece closes arguing that the supply-side infrastructure (app stores, platform liability shields) must be addressed before any demand-side harm reduction (deleting school photos) can be meaningful.
points: The UK National Crime Agency now advises schools to remove student photographs from public websites because pupils are using AI nudifier tools on class photos -- a demand-side response that leaves the supply (app stores distributing the apps) entirely untouched.

The Almendralejo precedent set the cost of AI-generated CSAM at 1,200 euros -- the largest sanction yet -- while the app used (ClothOff) continues to operate, demonstrating that legal deterrence is functionally nonexistent.

The Motherless precedent -- 18 years of documented harm under Section 230 protection, ended not by regulators but by press investigation, then partially restored within days -- is the structural model now operating inside every app store.

Nudify apps have been downloaded 483 million times and generated $122 million in revenue despite published policy bans from both Apple and Google, with both stores serving paid advertisements for the same apps even after announced removals.

The author's core structural argument: nudify apps represent not an enforcement gap but a profit-sharing arrangement -- app stores earn revenue from policy-violating apps and then perform removal theater under press pressure, repeating the Motherless cycle.
quotes: UK schools are now being told to remove students' photographs from their public websites. The reason is plain: criminals are scraping ordinary class photos, feeding them through AI nudifier tools, and using the resulting images for blackmail. Children in primary schools are now using the same tools on their classmates.

ClothOff is still operating. The structural shape is the lesson: a platform provides the infrastructure, the harm is produced by individual users, the platform invokes user-generated-content defences. Enforcement takes 18 years to catch up.

Nudify apps have collectively been downloaded around 483 million times, despite policy bans. They have generated more than $122 million in global revenue. Against the largest sanction yet issued, 1,200 euros in Spain.

The infrastructure has moved from a single hosted site to every smartphone, distributed by the two app stores that govern digital commerce for the majority of the world's population. The Motherless playbook is now in every school.
The first response is to delete the photographs. The supply of the technology that made the harm possible is untouched. Eighteen years of operation, and even the takedown was partial.

In early 2026, the Tech Transparency Project documented 47 nudify apps available in Apple's App Store and 55 in Google Play, despite both companies' published policies forbidding them. Both companies were still serving paid advertisements for nudify apps in their own search results after the removals.
